title: Parents
hookLine: honor them, including when it's complicated
tomorrow: why do brothers in the Bible fight so much?

cards: A text from a parent: call me when you can. Your stomach does something before you even know why. Maybe it's love, maybe it's an old argument, maybe both.
So what do you owe a parent when it's complicated? The commandment is short, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Honour thy father and thy mother." Notice what it doesn't say.
It doesn't say agree with them. It doesn't say like them every day. It says honor.

teach.h: I MUST BE IN MY FATHER'S HOUSE.
teach.b: Luke tells a story where honor and honesty sit in the same scene. Jesus is twelve. His parents lose him on the road home from Jerusalem and find him days later in the Temple.
His mother says what any parent would: we've been looking for you, sick with worry. He answers honestly: didn't you know I had to be in my Father's house? They don't understand him.
And then, in the Douay-Rheims words: "he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them." Both things, in one family. Luke adds that his mother kept all these words in her heart.
She didn't understand her son yet, and she didn't stop holding on to him either. Honesty on one side, patience on the other, and nobody walks out. The Catechism draws the same lines.
Children living at home obey their parents in what is good, but if conscience says an order is wrong, they must not follow it.
Grown children owe respect, gratitude, and help when parents are old, sick or lonely. The book of Sirach adds patience: if a father's understanding fails, don't look down on him.
So honor isn't pretending, and it isn't a performance of agreement at the dinner table. It's telling the truth and staying respectful while you do.
And if a parent caused real harm, honor can be as small as a prayer said from a safe distance.

how: Catholics count honoring father and mother among the Ten Commandments; the Catechism spells it out as respect, gratitude, obedience at home within the limits of conscience, and care for parents in old age.

o: the ones you must agree with until you leave home
anyone older who gives you advice about life
the ones you honor honestly, even when it's hard

s: the commandment says obey your father and mother
it says honor. the Catechism adds that conscience comes first when an order is wrong.
in Luke, the twelve-year-old Jesus went home and was subject to his parents
after telling them honestly where he had to be.
the Catechism says grown children owe nothing more once they leave home
it names respect, gratitude, and help in old age, sickness and loneliness.

games.q: your mom keeps sharing health posts you know are false, and she's hurt when you correct her. what honors her honestly?
o: repost one now and then so she feels supported.
mute her, and quietly stop bringing it up at all.
tell her privately and kindly, and keep calling her.
games.why: honor isn't pretending, and it isn't pulling away. in Luke, Jesus says the honest thing and still goes home with his parents.

practice: Say your parents' names out loud, quietly, one at a time, living or gone, and the names of anyone who raised you. After each name, let one true thing come up, a thank-you or a hurt, without arguing with it.
If you pray, pray for each of them by name, just as they are today.

wordCard.voice: Parents. The ones the commandment asks you to honor, not to pretend about. Today's word.

orig.s: Honora patrem tuum et matrem tuam
orig.say: oh-NOH-rah PAH-trem TOO-oom et MAH-trem TOO-ahm
orig.note: Latin, from the Vulgate: honor your father and your mother.

carryVoice: Your line: honor, honestly. At twelve, Jesus told the truth and still went home with them. See you tomorrow.
